name: v4
about: Calibration of the v4 body (HumanoidV4Builder in body.py): the v3 body (average young man, 1.75 m / 67.5 kg, series-elastic Achilles and quadriceps) with the parameters the literature check of 2026-09-28 found unrealistic changed to literature values. Every value was set from its sources before any speed was measured on it; none is tuned to reach a speed. Only changes with verified or derived evidence are applied; parameters the check found realistic or generous stay at their v3 values (`kept`), and changes resting on modelling convention or weak evidence are recorded but not applied (`uncertain_not_applied`, with their measured effect on the ideal-control ceiling). `verified`: the numbers were read in the source (true), derived from verified numbers ('derived'), or rest on modelling convention or weak evidence ('uncertain').

tendon_scale.unit: multiplier on the v3 quadriceps series stiffness (250 N/mm at 4.5 cm): 4.0 = 1000 N/mm
evidence: whole vasti series elasticity in OpenSim models, from the model files: ~976 N/mm (gait2392), ~927 N/mm (Rajagopal 2016)

patellar tendon stiffness in vivo: 1076 N/mm (O'Brien et al. 2010), 2826 (Helland et al. 2013), 3185-3269 (Bojsen-Moller et al. 2007), 3622 (Couppe et al. 2012), 4334 (Hansen et al. 2006); the whole muscle-tendon series (tendon plus aponeurosis) is more compliant than the free tendon, so the models' ~1000 N/mm is taken
Achilles kept at 200 N/mm (188 +- 43 in hopping, Lichtwark & Wilson 2005; 306-319, Rosager et al. 2002)

omega_muscle.unit: unloaded joint angular velocity of one muscle direction, rad/s (hip_flex_neg = hip extensors: gluteus maximus and, through their hip action, the hamstrings; hip_flex_pos = hip flexors: iliopsoas and, through its hip action, rectus femoris); MuJoCo vmax = omega * 0.3 / joint range
evidence: w0 = fibre vmax x optimal fibre length / moment arm with the standard models' fibre vmax of 10 L0/s (OpenSim Thelen2003 default, gait2392, Hamner 2010, Rajagopal 2016; Arnold & Delp 2011) and Ward et al. 2009's fibre lengths: PCSA-weighted hip extensors ~18.5 rad/s, hip flexors ~29 rad/s (at 15 L0/s, the high-speed models' value: ~28 and ~44); the standard 10 L0/s values are taken

the v3 value (15 for both) is below what sprinting needs: 79 sprinters at 9.9 m/s reach hip extension 850 +- 73 deg/s (14.8 rad/s) in stance and thigh lift 792 deg/s (13.8 rad/s) in swing (Miyashiro et al. 2019, PMC7739839), where a w0 of 15 leaves the muscles ~0 % of their force
omega_muscle.verified: derived (fibre vmax and fibre lengths verified in the model files and Ward 2009; hip moment arms typical values)

kept.peak torques: the v3 isometric capacities are 1.4-2.9x young men's voluntary maxima (Anderson et al. 2007; Maden-Wilkinson et al. 2020; Krantz et al. 2020), as in common modelling practice (Rajagopal 2016 notes models exceed voluntary maxima; sprint simulations double Fmax): kept, not raised
kept.force-velocity shape: MuJoCo's quadratic keeps more force at every velocity than Hill (a/F0 0.25-0.30) or De Groote 2016 curves: generous, kept
kept.force-length: 0.75-1.05 of L0 over the joint range with lmin 0.5 keeps 50 % at the short end where human muscles keep 10-35 % (Anderson 2007; Maganaris 2001, 2003): generous, kept
kept.activation: 10 / 40 ms (Millard 2013, OpenSim defaults; 10 / 30 in sprint simulations, Chumanov et al. 2011): kept
kept.segments: masses match Dempster / Winter (de Leva 1996's thigh includes the buttock); joint-to-joint lengths hip-knee 0.43 m and knee-ankle 0.43 m match de Leva scaled to 1.75 m (0.424 / 0.436): kept
kept.friction and planarity: foot friction 1.2 adequate; arm swing mainly cancels vertical-axis angular momentum (Hinrichs 1987) and folding the arms slows a 30 m sprint by 1.6 % (Brooks, Weyand & Clark 2022): the planar model loses a few percent at most, kept
kept.not modelled yet: series elasticity of the hamstrings, rectus femoris and gastrocnemius separately from the Achilles group (tendon slack / fibre length 3-7 in Delp / Rajagopal models; Rajagopal makes them compliant)

joint speeds.ankle: NOT changed (20 rad/s kept): the soleus's fibres alone give ~9-13 rad/s at 10-15 L0/s, so the v3 plantarflexor fibres (20) are already fast; the observed 17.6 rad/s plantarflexion (Miyashiro 2019) comes with tendon recoil (~26 rad/s unloaded with a pre-loaded tendon, Beaumatin et al. 2018), which v3's elastic Achilles models
joint speeds.knee: NOT changed (25 kept): vasti w0 20-25 rad/s at 10 L0/s; fitted knee-extension w0 17.5 +- 8.5 rad/s (Hauraix et al. 2017)

human_targets.how: every number read in the source (verified), read off a plotted figure (fig-read), or calculated from verified numbers (derived); sources fetched directly (Europe PMC / PMC full texts, Wayback copies of J Appl Physiol, the World Athletics London 2017 report)

top speed.from: Lazarczuk et al. 2025 (PMC12552802): 7.77 +- 0.86 SD, recreationally active, radar; Clark, Meng & Stearne 2020 (Biol Open, Table 2): 8.23 +- 0.13 SEM, slower half of 20 active males

contact / aerial.value: 0.130 / 0.109 s (Clark 2020); 0.120 / 0.124 s from Weyand et al. 2000's regressions at 8.0 m/s

mean vertical force in contact.value: 2.07 body weights at 8.0 m/s (Weyand 2000: 1.26 + 0.101 v); 1.99 in athlete non-sprinters (Clark & Weyand 2014)

peak vertical force.value: ~3.2 body weights (athlete non-sprinters' averaged waveform, Clark & Weyand 2014 Fig. 7A); no direct untrained measurement

top speed.from: mean + 1.645 SD with the observed SDs 0.4-0.9 m/s (Lazarczuk 2025, Clark 2020, Lenthall et al. 2024)

top speed.value: 9.90 +- 0.46 m/s; contact 0.103-0.105 s, flight 0.112-0.115 s, step 2.15 m at 4.60 /s, swing 0.330 s; hip extension 850 +- 73 deg/s in stance, thigh lift 792 deg/s
top speed.from: Miyashiro et al. 2019 (PMC7739839): 79 sprinters, 1.75 m / 66.6 kg

forces.value: mean 2.30, peak 3.93 +- 0.51 body weights at 10.8 m/s

top speed.from: Krzysztof & Mero 2013 (PMC3661886); Bissas et al. 2018 World Athletics report

fvmax.unit: eccentric force plateau (x isometric), MuJoCo muscle fvmax
evidence: muscle models use 1.4 (Millard et al. 2013, Rajagopal 2016) to 1.79-1.8 (De Groote et al. 2016 source; Thelen Flen in gait2392); 1.6 is the middle
a small lever for speed: Miller, Umberger & Caldwell 2012 found 6.23-6.70 m/s over the eccentric plateau's range
fvmax.verified: uncertain (modelling convention; no direct human measurement of the whole-muscle plateau)
fvmax.probe: average body, pitch-free ideal-control ceiling: +1.0 m/s on the margin probe (~8.2-8.5 against 7.0-7.35), +0.9 and +0.2 on the two stance-budget screens: among the larger levers, and the least grounded; kept at the v3 value until human whole-muscle eccentric capacity in vivo is pinned down

foot_solref.unit: MuJoCo contact solref on the feet: [time constant s, damping ratio]
evidence: MuJoCo's default contact is critically damped with a 20 ms time constant, ~20 % of a 0.10 s sprint stance, i.e. a very soft foot-ground interface (whole-body effective stiffness ~170 kN/m); human heel pad ~150 kN/m in vivo (Aerts et al. 1995) and 32-212 N/mm in walking (Wearing et al. 2014), sprint surfaces 75-946 kN/m (Kerdok et al. 2002); the suggested range is 0.005-0.01 s, checked against the force rise and a peak near 3.5-4 body weights at top speed (Weyand et al. 2010: 3.6; Weyand et al. 2009: 3.93 +- 0.51)
0.01 is the soft end of that range (twice the 1 ms timestep's 2x floor)
foot_solref.verified: uncertain (validated below by the peak force, not by a direct measurement of contact softness)
foot_solref.probe: 0.01 s: -0.6 m/s on the margin probe, -0.2 and -1.2 on the two stance-budget screens (stiffer contact raises the impact peaks the analysis caps at 5 body weights); kept at MuJoCo's default

probe.method: sprint_limits.py speeds --pitch-free (no pitch stabiliser in stance), chained upward from 5 m/s in 0.5 m/s steps from one warm start. Two ceilings: (1) margin: the fastest speed whose swing-time margin tc + 2 taer - t_sw stays positive (the better of two optimisations per speed, two chains); (2) stance budget: where the best penalised stance budget tc + 2 taer falls to a human swing time of 0.35 s (Weyand et al. 2000: 0.373 +- 0.03; sprinters 0.33-0.36), which needs no swing optimisation and is steadier. Single points carry +-0.3-0.5 m/s.
probe.reading: what bounds the ideal-control top speed is the vertical impulse a short stance can deliver: the knee- and ankle-extensor strength move the ceiling most (+2 m/s for x1.5), then the force-length width, while hip speed, the quadriceps tendon and friction give +0.4-0.6 each and a stiffer foot contact costs speed (impact peaks against the analysis's 5 body-weight cap). Only the hip speeds and the quadriceps stiffness have literature support for a change: the model's knee and ankle extensor capacities are already 1.5-3x young men's voluntary maxima (Anderson et al. 2007; Maden-Wilkinson et al. 2020) and its force-length curve is already generous at short lengths (0.5 of isometric at the short end, 0.1-0.35 measured: Anderson 2007; Maganaris 2001, 2003), so neither is raised.
probe.not probed: the planar constraint (the analysis is planar by construction; the literature puts the arms' and pelvis rotation's contribution at a few percent: Hinrichs 1987; Brooks, Weyand & Clark 2022) and the foot's geometry (the MTP joint is modelled; Stefanyshyn & Nigg 1997 find it absorbs energy in sprinting and generates almost none)

screen.how: average body, one change at a time on v3; stance-budget ceiling at t_sw 0.35 (m/s); ONE chain with one optimisation per speed, so a row carries about +-0.5-0.7 m/s (v4b on one chain: 7.46; on two: 8.2). Two screens were run (b2: 2026-09-28 morning; s5: after v4b was fixed); only the strength and force-length rows stand clear of that noise.

omega.why: a first reading of the literature check (hip 30 for both directions, ankle 27) took the high-speed models' 15 L0/s end for the hip and the recoil-assisted plantarflexion speed for the fibres; its average-body ceiling was ~9.0-9.7 m/s on the better of two chains. Replaced by the standard-model values above before any sprinter was tuned on it.

average body (v4).margin chains: positive to 8.5 and to 6.5 m/s (two chains)

human, untrained men.at ~8 m/s: contact 0.120-0.130, aerial 0.109-0.124, step 1.96-2.00 m, rate 3.96-4.21 /s, mean force 2.07, peak ~2.8-3.6 (Clark, Meng & Stearne 2020; Weyand et al. 2000 regressions; Clark & Weyand 2014)

average body (v4).verdict: top speed and contact time in the human range; the ideal-control gait flies ~25 % longer, steps ~10 % longer at ~10 % lower rate, with ~6 % more mean and ~40 % more peak vertical force than humans (the optimiser uses the 5 body-weight cap the analysis allows)

P95 (v4).human: untrained 95th percentile ~8.8-9.2 m/s (mean + 1.645 SD); trained sprinters 9.90 +- 0.46 (Miyashiro et al. 2019: contact 0.103, flight 0.113, step 2.15 m at 4.60 /s)
P95 (v4).verdict: above the untrained 95th percentile, near trained sprinters; the p95 profile is a composite (every part at its own 95th percentile at once)

elite2 (v4).verdict: far below elite sprinters, and below v4 P95: elite2 keeps knee and ankle extensors per kg near the untrained mean (the literature), and those are what the ceiling is most sensitive to; what else makes elites fast is not in this model (candidate: stance technique or tendon properties beyond the Achilles)
